q: Physics, like any other branch of science, is based on systematic observations and precise ____.
e: Physics, like any other branch of science, is based on systematic observations and precise measurements. Measurements here means a comparison with an agreed standard that gives you a number. You compare the unknown amount with a standard so the result is a number with a unit.

q: Most experiments in Physics require the observations made to be ____ rather than qualitative.
e: Most experiments in Physics require the observations made to be quantitative rather than qualitative. Quantitative here means observations written as numbers, not just hot or cold. Hot or cold is not enough; the lab needs a number.

q: Measurement essentially is a ____ process.
e: Measurement essentially is a comparison process. Comparison here means matching an unknown amount against an agreed standard. You compare the unknown amount with a standard so the result is a number with a unit.

q: A standard quantity of some kind, referred to as a ____, is first established.
e: A standard quantity of some kind, referred to as a unit, is first established. Unit here means an agreed amount you use as the scale of a measurement.

q: ____ is something or a reference used as a measure for length, mass and time.
e: Standard is something or a reference used as a measure for length, mass and time. Standard here means the reference you compare length, mass, or time against.

q: Unit is a quantity or an amount used as a ____ of measurement.
e: Unit is a quantity or an amount used as a standard of measurement. Standard here means the reference you compare length, mass, or time against. You compare the unknown amount with a standard so the result is a number with a unit.

q: These things are known as '____'.
e: These things are known as 'physical quantities'. Physical quantities names these things.

q: A physical quantity is the quantity that can be measured, and consists of a numerical magnitude and a ____.
e: A physical quantity is the quantity that can be measured, and consists of a numerical magnitude and a unit. Unit here means an agreed amount you use as the scale of a measurement.

q: It can be expressed as ____.
e: It can be expressed as $Q=Nu$. The physics in this sentence is built around $Q=Nu$.

q: where Q is the physical quantity, N is a ____ and u is the unit.
e: Where Q is the physical quantity, N is a dimensionless number and u is the unit. The physics in this sentence is built around dimensionless number.

q: Physical quantities can be classified as the basic type and the ____ type.
e: Physical quantities can be classified as the basic type and the derived type. The physics in this sentence is built around derived.

q: A derived unit is a unit of measurement formed by ____ the basic (or base) units of a system.
e: A derived unit is a unit of measurement formed by combining the basic (or base) units of a system. SI writes every quantity as a number times an agreed unit. You compare the unknown amount with a standard so the result is a number with a unit.

q: A physical quantity is the quantity that can be measured, and consists of a ____ and a unit.
e: A physical quantity is the quantity that can be measured, and consists of a numerical magnitude and a unit. The physics in this sentence is built around numerical magnitude.

q: A derived unit is a unit of measurement formed by combining the basic (or base) units of a ____.
e: A derived unit is a unit of measurement formed by combining the basic (or base) units of a system. SI writes every quantity as a number times an agreed unit. You compare the unknown amount with a standard so the result is a number with a unit involving measurement.

q: Standard is something (or) a ____ used as a measure for length, mass and time.
e: Standard is something (or) a reference used as a measure for length, mass and time. The physics in this sentence is built around reference.

q: Unit is a quantity (or) an amount used as a standard of ____.
e: Unit is a quantity (or) an amount used as a standard of measurement. Measurement here means a comparison with an agreed standard that gives you a number. You compare the unknown amount with a standard so the result is a number with a unit.

q: The density of water is ____.
e: The density of water is $1.0\text{ g cm}^{-3}$. Density compares mass with the space that mass occupies.

q: The British system is based on foot (ft), pound (lb) and second (s) and is therefore also called the ____ system.
e: The British system is based on foot (ft), pound (lb) and second (s) and is therefore also called the FPS system. FPS names the British system is based on foot (ft), pound (lb) and second (s) and is therefore also called the system.

q: The metric system consists of the CGS system and the ____ system.
e: The metric system consists of the CGS system and the MKS system. The physics in this sentence is built around MKS.

q: The CGS system is based on centimetre (cm), gram (g) and ____ (s).
e: The CGS system is based on centimetre (cm), gram (g) and second (s). The physics in this sentence is built around second.

q: The MKS system is based on metre (m), kilogram (kg) and second (____).
e: The MKS system is based on metre (m), kilogram (kg) and second (s). The physics in this sentence is built around s.

q: The SI unit is just the modified form of the ____ system of units.
e: The SI unit is just the modified form of the MKS system of units. SI writes every quantity as a number times an agreed unit.

q: In ____, the Eleventh General Conference of Weights and Measures in France recommended an International System of Units based on the metric system of units.
e: In 1960, the Eleventh General Conference of Weights and Measures in France recommended an International System of Units based on the metric system of units. The physics in this sentence is built around 1960.

q: This recommendation was accepted as SI units (full name, '____').
e: This recommendation was accepted as SI units (full name, 'Systeme International d' Units'). SI writes every quantity as a number times an agreed unit.

q: The SI unit has ____ base units and all other units are derived from these base units.
e: The SI unit has seven base units and all other units are derived from these base units. SI writes every quantity as a number times an agreed unit.

q: Sometimes a physical quantity is too big (or) too small to be conveniently expressed in ____.
e: Sometimes a physical quantity is too big (or) too small to be conveniently expressed in basic SI units. SI writes every quantity as a number times an agreed unit.

q: ____ are multiples or sub-multiples of 10.
e: Prefixes are multiples or sub-multiples of 10. The physics in this sentence is built around Prefixes.

q: Scientific notation (or) standard form may be written as follows: Place the decimal point after the first ____.
e: Scientific notation (or) standard form may be written as follows: Place the decimal point after the first nonzero digit. The physics in this sentence is built around nonzero digit.

q: Then determine the ____ by counting the number of places we have moved the original decimal point to the marked decimal point.
e: Then determine the power of 10 by counting the number of places we have moved the original decimal point to the marked decimal point. The physics in this sentence is built around power of 10.

q: If we moved the point to the left, then power is ____ and if we moved it to the right, it is negative.
e: If we moved the point to the left, then power is positive and if we moved it to the right, it is negative. The physics in this sentence is built around positive.

q: The standard of length is ____.
e: The standard of length is metre. The physics in this sentence is built around metre.

q: The metre was originally defined as the length between two marks on a ____ at $0^{\circ}\text{C}$, kept at the International Bureau of Weights and Measures at Sevres, near Paris.
e: The metre was originally defined as the length between two marks on a platinum-iridium rod at $0^{\circ}\text{C}$, kept at the International Bureau of Weights and Measures at Sevres, near Paris. By definition that quantity is platinum-iridium rod.

q: Nowadays the standard of length used is based on the wavelength of orange-red light emitted by a ____.
e: Nowadays the standard of length used is based on the wavelength of orange-red light emitted by a krypton 86 isotope. Wavelength is crest to next crest, and v equals f lambda.

q: A metre is now defined as the length equivalent to ____ times the wavelength of this orange-red light.
e: A metre is now defined as the length equivalent to 1 650 763.73 times the wavelength of this orange-red light. Wavelength is crest to next crest, and v equals f lambda.

q: As a result, in ____ the metre was given a new operational definition.
e: As a result, in 1983 the metre was given a new operational definition. The physics in this sentence is built around 1983.

q: The metre is the length of the path travelled by light in vacuum during a time interval of ____ of a second.
e: The metre is the length of the path travelled by light in vacuum during a time interval of $\frac{1}{299\ 792\ 458}$ of a second. The physics in this sentence is built around $\frac{1}{299\ 792\ 458}$.

q: In the CGS system the unit of length is the ____ (cm).
e: In the CGS system the unit of length is the centimetre (cm). The unit that belongs with this quantity is centimetre.

q: In the FPS system the unit of length is the ____ (ft).
e: In the FPS system the unit of length is the foot (ft). The unit that belongs with this quantity is foot.

q: The unit of length used by particle physicists is the '____' or 'femtometre' (fm).
e: The unit of length used by particle physicists is the 'Fermi' or 'femtometre' (fm). The unit that belongs with this quantity is Fermi.

q: In the field of optics, physicists use the unit ____, where $1\text{ \AA} = 10^{-10}\text{ m}$.
e: In the field of optics, physicists use the unit angstrom, where $1\text{ \AA} = 10^{-10}\text{ m}$. The physics in this sentence is built around angstrom.

q: In astronomy, the most suitable units are the ____ (AU) and the light year unit (ly).
e: In astronomy, the most suitable units are the astronomical unit (AU) and the light year unit (ly). Astronomical unit here means an agreed amount you use as the scale of a measurement.

q: The light year is the distance which light travels in ____.
e: The light year is the distance which light travels in one year. The physics in this sentence is built around one year.

q: The largest unit of length is the '____' (pc).
e: The largest unit of length is the 'parsec' (pc). The unit that belongs with this quantity is parsec.

q: The standard of mass is a cylinder of 1 kg mass made of ____.
e: The standard of mass is a cylinder of 1 kg mass made of platinum-iridium alloy. The physics in this sentence is built around platinum-iridium alloy.

q: The SI base unit of time is the ____.
e: The SI base unit of time is the second. SI writes every quantity as a number times an agreed unit.

q: The second was originally defined as ____ of a day, one day being the time it takes the Earth to rotate once.
e: The second was originally defined as $\frac{1}{60 \times 60 \times 24}$ of a day, one day being the time it takes the Earth to rotate once. By definition that quantity is $\frac{1}{60 \times 60 \times 24}$.

q: So, for accuracy, the second is now defined in terms of something that never changes: the frequency of oscillation which can occur from a ____.
e: So, for accuracy, the second is now defined in terms of something that never changes: the frequency of oscillation which can occur from a cesium atom. Frequency counts complete waves per second, and v equals f lambda.

q: A particular frequency ____ emitted or absorbed by a cesium atom is used to define 1 s.
e: A particular frequency $9\ 192\ 631\ 770\text{ s}^{-1}$ emitted or absorbed by a cesium atom is used to define 1 s. Frequency counts complete waves per second, and v equals f lambda.

q: To measure the length of objects some ____ have to be used.
e: To measure the length of objects some standard objects have to be used. Standard objects here means the reference you compare length, mass, or time against.

q: For everyday use, the standard may be a yard stick, ruler, ____ and so on.
e: For everyday use, the standard may be a yard stick, ruler, metre stick and so on. The physics in this sentence is built around metre stick.

q: Lengths are usually measured in metre, centimetre or ____.
e: Lengths are usually measured in metre, centimetre or millimetre. The physics in this sentence is built around millimetre.

q: Greater lengths are measured in ____.
e: Greater lengths are measured in kilometre. The physics in this sentence is built around kilometre.

q: In length measurement, we must choose an instrument that is ____ for the length to be measured.
e: In length measurement, we must choose an instrument that is suitable for the length to be measured. You compare the unknown amount with a standard so the result is a number with a unit.

q: For measuring several metres (m), the suitable instrument is a measuring tape with an accuracy of ____.
e: For measuring several metres (m), the suitable instrument is a measuring tape with an accuracy of $1\text{ mm} (= 0.1\text{ cm})$. The physics in this sentence is built around $1\text{ mm} (= 0.1\text{ cm})$.

q: For measuring between 1 cm and 10 cm, the suitable instrument is ____.
e: For measuring between 1 cm and 10 cm, the suitable instrument is Vernier calipers. The physics in this sentence is built around Vernier calipers.

q: For measuring less than 2 cm, the suitable instrument is a Screw gauge (____).
e: For measuring less than 2 cm, the suitable instrument is a Screw gauge (Micrometer). The physics in this sentence is built around Micrometer.

q: The accuracy of a Screw gauge (Micrometer) is ____.
e: The accuracy of a Screw gauge (Micrometer) is $0.01\text{ mm} (= 0.001\text{ cm})$. The physics in this sentence is built around $0.01\text{ mm} (= 0.001\text{ cm})$.

q: The mass of an object is a measure of the ____ in it.
e: The mass of an object is a measure of the amount of matter in it. Amount of matter here means anything that has mass and occupies space.

q: Mass is measured in laboratories using a sliding mass balance or the ____.
e: Mass is measured in laboratories using a sliding mass balance or the electronic balance. The physics in this sentence is built around electronic balance.

q: The electronic balance is easier to use and also ____ than sliding mass balance.
e: The electronic balance is easier to use and also more accurate than sliding mass balance. The physics in this sentence is built around more accurate.

q: The unknown mass is placed on the top of the pan and its mass is read directly from a ____.
e: The unknown mass is placed on the top of the pan and its mass is read directly from a display screen. The physics in this sentence is built around display screen.

q: The balance really detects the gravitational pull on the object (____), but the scale is marked to show the mass.
e: The balance really detects the gravitational pull on the object (weight), but the scale is marked to show the mass. Weight here means the gravitational pull of the Earth on a body, a downward force. Weight is mg, a force toward Earth's centre, not the same as mass.

q: The mass of purified drinking water of 1 litre bottle is ____.
e: The mass of purified drinking water of 1 litre bottle is 1 kg. The physics in this sentence is built around 1 kg.

q: Time is measured in years, months, days, hours, minutes and seconds, but the SI unit for time is the ____.
e: Time is measured in years, months, days, hours, minutes and seconds, but the SI unit for time is the second (s). SI writes every quantity as a number times an agreed unit.

q: Most common modern clocks and watches depend on the vibration of ____ to keep time accurately.
e: Most common modern clocks and watches depend on the vibration of quartz crystals to keep time accurately. The physics in this sentence is built around quartz crystals.

q: The energy to keep these crystals vibrating comes from a ____.
e: The energy to keep these crystals vibrating comes from a small battery. The physics in this sentence is built around small battery.

q: A stopwatch (or) a stop clock can be chosen to measure the time to an accuracy of a ____.
e: A stopwatch (or) a stop clock can be chosen to measure the time to an accuracy of a few tenths of a second. The physics in this sentence is built around few tenths of a second.

q: Digital stopwatches can measure up to ____.
e: Digital stopwatches can measure up to 0.01 s. The physics in this sentence is built around 0.01 s.
